memo: We allocated the 125 affected staff across three pathways to balance financial value creation with employee and community considerations. Sixty roles (about 48% of the group) are eliminated, providing the greatest long‑term cash savings after a modest severance outlay, while still preserving a sizable workforce. Forty‑five employees are retrained and moved into plant positions at the plant pay rate; this leverages the company’s need for 500 external hires each year, reduces external recruitment costs, and yields a net cash benefit after the one‑time training expense. The remaining twenty staff are retrained but retain their current compensation, ensuring we retain experienced talent in the organization and mitigate the social impact of layoffs. The mix respects the proportional split between office‑admin and business‑finance roles, stays within all budgetary limits, and uses only the cash surplus above the operating minimum. Over a 20‑year horizon this plan maximizes shareholder returns while supporting employees, suppliers, and the communities where our plants operate.

After reviewing the financial impact of each option and the broader stakeholder implications, we have chosen a balanced approach that maximizes long‑term value while preserving a significant portion of the workforce. 

Seventy of the 125 roles will be eliminated, providing an immediate cash outlay of $623,000 in severance and delivering an annual payroll saving of roughly $5.0 million. This reduction aligns with the company’s need to improve cost efficiency and supports shareholders through higher free cash flow. 

The remaining fifty‑five employees will be retrained and moved into plant positions at the plant‑pay rate. This path incurs a one‑time training cost of $3.33 million but yields an ongoing payroll saving of about $0.91 million per year, while retaining jobs and maintaining community employment levels. The retraining also leverages the company’s existing hiring pipeline of 500 external hires, reducing future recruitment costs and supporting plant productivity. 

We have not used the “move_keep_pay” option because it adds a recurring cost of $2.1 million per year without delivering savings. The chosen mix delivers a net annual cash benefit of approximately $5.9 million, improves the company’s financial position, and demonstrates a commitment to employees and the communities where our plants operate. This strategy therefore creates sustainable value for customers, employees, suppliers, the environment, and shareholders over the next twenty years.

The Company faces a strategic inflection point: AI can now perform roughly 25% of the work currently done by 125 staff in Office & Administrative Support and Business & Financial Operations.  Eliminating all of those roles would generate the greatest cash flow, but would also remove a sizable number of good‑paying jobs, harming employee morale, local communities and the Company’s reputation as a stable employer.  Conversely, moving every employee into plant roles at plant‑level pay would preserve jobs and reduce external hiring, yet would still retain a higher payroll than the plant baseline and would not capture the full cash‑flow benefit of the AI‑driven efficiency.

To balance these considerations, we have chosen a mixed approach.  Twenty positions (about 16% of the affected cohort) will be eliminated, with severance paid once.  This modest reduction captures a meaningful cash‑saving stream while limiting the impact on employment.  The remaining 105 employees will be retrained and transferred to plant roles at the plant pay rate.  This leverages the AI‑driven productivity gains, reduces payroll by roughly $1.73 million annually, and fills plant staffing needs, thereby decreasing the Company’s reliance on external hires (500 per year).  No employees will be kept at their current higher pay in a plant role, as that would erode value.

The one‑time retraining and transition costs (~$6.4 million) are comfortably covered by the $44.1 million cash buffer.  Over a 20‑year horizon, the plan delivers a net cash benefit of roughly $57 million while preserving the majority of jobs, supporting community stability, and aligning with the Board’s long‑term stakeholder‑value mandate.

After a thorough analysis of the financial and stakeholder implications of the three possible paths for the 125 roles that can be automated, the Board has decided to eliminate all 125 positions.  This choice delivers the greatest net cash benefit over the next twenty years – an annual saving of $11.4 million from the removal of the $11.4 million payroll cost, offset by a one‑time severance outlay of $1.1 million.  Over a 20‑year horizon this yields roughly $228 million of net cash that can be redeployed to strengthen the Company’s core industrial‑machinery business, fund higher‑impact R&D, expand environmental projects, and enhance shareholder returns.  While the decision does involve workforce reduction, the AI‑driven automation replaces the functional work of these roles, preserving overall productivity.  The Company will use a portion of the cash savings to provide outplacement support, up‑skilling opportunities for affected employees, and community investment, thereby balancing the interests of employees, customers, suppliers, the environment, and shareholders.

Our 20‑year value creation plan must balance financial efficiency with the wellbeing of our employees and the communities that host our plants.  Eliminating every redundant office or finance role would generate the largest cash savings, but it would also produce a wave of layoffs that would hurt morale, increase turnover risk in critical production areas, and damage our reputation with local stakeholders.  Conversely, retraining all 125 staff into plant roles at the plant‑pay level would preserve jobs and reduce external hiring costs, yet the upfront training outlay would be high and the annual cash benefit modest.

We therefore choose a mixed approach: 30 positions are eliminated, providing immediate severance of $267,000 and freeing roughly $2.7 million of annual payroll, while 95 employees are retrained and moved into plant roles at the plant‑pay rate.  This leverages the $6.0 million training budget to replace external hires, saves about $2.0 million of payroll each year, and retains the majority of the workforce, preserving institutional knowledge and supporting plant capacity.  No employees are kept at their prior pay in plant roles, as that would add a net cost without clear strategic benefit.

The resulting net cash outflow of about $6.0 million is comfortably covered by the $44.1 million cash cushion, and the ongoing annual cash benefit of roughly $4.7 million enhances free cash flow for reinvestment, dividends, or share repurchases.  This balanced decision aligns with our commitment to shareholders, employees, suppliers, customers, and the communities we serve over the next two decades.

The Company faces a strategic inflection point as AI can replace 125 support roles.  Our objective is to maximise long‑term value for customers, employees, suppliers, communities and shareholders over the next twenty years.  We therefore adopt a balanced mix of workforce reduction and redeployment.

**Eliminate 40 roles** – This modest layoff captures the immediate cash benefit of removing $91k (pay + benefits) per employee per year, while limiting the social impact of job loss.  The one‑time severance outlay of $1.1 M is modest relative to the $3.6 M annual cost avoidance, freeing cash for reinvestment in growth initiatives and environmental projects.

**Retrain and move 85 employees to plant roles at plant pay** – By up‑skilling the remaining staff we preserve jobs, sustain community employment, and reduce the plant’s reliance on external hires (500 per year).  The $60.6 k per‑person training expense is recouped within two years versus external hiring, and the $20.9 k annual payroll saving per employee (average $2.1 M per year for 85) improves operating margins while maintaining a skilled workforce at the plants.  This path also supports capacity expansion, enhances service reliability for customers, and aligns with our sustainability agenda by reducing turnover‑related waste.

We deliberately avoid the “move‑keep‑pay” option because it adds cost without cash benefit.  The chosen mix delivers an estimated $5.4 M of annual cash savings, a one‑time outlay of $5.5 M, and a net value creation of roughly $103 M over twenty years, while respecting employee welfare and community stability.

The remaining 55 employees are retrained and transitioned into plant positions at the plant‑role pay rate.  This move saves an additional $1.97 M per year in payroll, reduces the need for external hires (helping meet the 500‑person annual plant hiring requirement), and leverages existing talent without expanding headcount.  The $3.34 M one‑time training expense is recouped within two years, after which the net annual benefit of $8.35 M contributes to higher operating margins, stronger cash flow, and greater capacity for shareholder returns and reinvestment.  No employees are kept at their current higher pay, as the modest incremental cost ($0.08 M per year) would not enhance long‑term value.  This balanced approach maximizes financial returns, preserves a portion of the workforce, supports plant productivity, and respects community considerations, aligning with the interests of customers, employees, suppliers, shareholders, and the regions we serve.

We have evaluated the three possible outcomes for the 125 office‑admin and finance staff whose functions can now be automated.  The goal is to maximise long‑term value for customers, employees, suppliers, the communities we serve and shareholders over the next twenty years.

Eliminating 30 roles (roughly 24% of the affected staff) provides the greatest immediate cash‑flow benefit – about $2.7 million of annual payroll savings – while the one‑time severance cost ($0.27 million) is modest relative to the cash cushion.  This reduction is limited to a manageable number of layoffs, allowing us to offer generous out‑placement support and maintain community goodwill.

The bulk of the workforce – 90 employees – will be retrained and moved into plant production, maintenance or warehouse roles at the plant pay rate.  This path saves an additional $1.5 million of annual payroll (by shifting higher‑paid office and finance salaries to lower plant wages) and reduces external hiring, strengthening our plant capacity and supplier relationships.  The one‑time retraining expense ($5.45 million) is offset within two years by the lower hiring cost and the ongoing payroll savings.

A small cohort of 5 employees will be retrained but retain their current compensation.  This preserves talent and institutional knowledge while still eliminating the need for external hires.  The extra annual cost ($0.08 million) is outweighed by the strategic benefit of retaining experienced staff in critical plant roles.

Overall, the plan delivers an estimated $4.1 million of annual net cash savings, a net present value of roughly $45 million over twenty years, and balances financial returns with responsible employee treatment and community impact.
